the plasma levels of sMAC are higher in PLWH with poor immune reconstituted compared to healthy individuals.
plasma sMAC is a potential biomarker for monitoring HIV‐related immunosuppression and that serum sMAC may have a role as a diagnostic biomarker in other disease settings.
plasma sMAC concentrations are higher in virally‐suppressed HIV patients with poor CD4+ T‐cell recovery than in HIV‐negative controls, with the highest levels seen in patients with low CD4+ T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sMAC assay is a useful and robust tool for measuring complement activation in a clinical setting and is a potential biomarker for monitoring HIV disease progression.

plasma sMAC is an important diagnostic marker for HIV patients, with higher sMAC levels correlating with poorer immune reconstitution, and that sMAC levels are higher in serum than in plasma, with no significant differences in sMAC levels between African American and Caucasian healthy donors.
sMAC levels in plasma and serum are significantly higher in HIV patients with low CD4+ T cells and that sMAC levels are significantly higher in serum than in plasma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plasma and serum levels are not interchangeable and must be carefully controlled for in any study involving sMAC.
sMAC levels can be used to monitor complement activation in the plasma and/or serum of patients, and may be useful in the monitoring and management of patients on antiviral therapy.
sMAC is a reliable biomarker that can be used to monitor complement activation in a variety of clinical settings.
